paras: The lynching of Mosier was the hanging of a man accused of murder by a mob that broke open the jail at Cheyenne, Wyoming Territory, sometime before 1888. According to a later account, seventy-five men took him from the jail on a Sunday night and hanged him from a telegraph pole before about 2,000 people, despite pleas from the Secretary of the Territory and the mayor. The Cheyenne Leader still cited the case in 1888 as a local precedent, and a railroad story reprinted that year called it "one of the most famous lynchings ever known in the far West."

The only detailed account is an anecdote from The Safety Valve, told by an unnamed Rocky Mountain delegate to a railroad Brotherhood convention and printed in 1888. In that telling, a man named "Moshier," described as "a low-lived assassin who had shot several people," was given a ride to Cheyenne by a freighter who was also carrying a young man bound for Iowa. During the night, while the party camped near Fort Russell about three miles from Cheyenne, Moshier was accused of striking both sleeping men with an axe and then shooting the passenger three times.

The passenger gave a dying statement but did not know his attacker's name, and he died that afternoon. Rewards were offered by the Territory and by private citizens, and "hundreds of men" searched the country until the freighter regained consciousness three days later and named the man.

Several days later the accused was captured by Sheriff Sweene of Fort Collins, Colorado. Because the Cheyenne sheriff "feared a lynching," a special Union Pacific train carrying Sheriff Sharpless, deputies, newspapermen and the road's superintendent was secretly sent to Fort Collins to bring the prisoner back before daylight. The party reached Cheyenne with him at sunrise on a Sunday.

That night, by the same account, seventy-five men "marched to the jail like a company of soldiers," broke open the doors and hanged the prisoner from a telegraph pole in the center of the city while some 2,000 people watched. Secretary Morgan, the Secretary of the Territory, and the mayor spoke to the mob and pleaded with it not to hang the man. The Cheyenne Leader later summarized the event in one line, writing that Mosier "was taken from custody of Sheriff Sharpless and lynched."

No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. The case remained a reference point in Cheyenne: in March 1888 a defense attorney in the Patterson ("Tin Hat") trial asked the arresting officer whether his prisoner had been afraid to come to Cheyenne "on account of the recent lynching of Mosier," a question the court ruled out. In December 1888, when a vigilance committee was said to be forming to lynch the killer of a man named Vannice, a rumor that the suspect was being held at Fort Russell drew color from the fact that Mosier had been taken from the sheriff and lynched.

No contemporary report of the lynching itself appears in the coverage, which consists of later references. The Cheyenne Leader mentioned Mosier only in passing, assuming its readers knew the case. The fullest version reached readers as a railroad yarn about the reckless engineer Fred Post, run in the Jackson Standard of Ohio in January 1888 and in the Abbeville Press and Banner of South Carolina in October under the subhead "A Lynching that was Only Postponed."

That story treated the hanging as the climax of the engineer's tale, calling the accused an "assassin" and the lynchers "avengers," while recording that territorial and city officials had tried to stop them. None of the accounts gives Mosier's race or first name.

The local paper spelled the name Mosier, while the railroad story printed "Moshier." The date is also unsettled: the railroad story gives no year, and the March 1888 trial question, which concerned an arrest made in 1885, called the lynching "recent."

bases: A crowd broke open the Cheyenne jail and hanged a man held for murder (A3), and the Cheyenne Leader recalled that Mosier was taken from the sheriff's custody and lynched (A6).

Seventy-five men broke open the jail and hanged Moshier, accused of an axe-and-pistol murder, while the territorial secretary and the mayor pleaded with them not to (A3); the Cheyenne Leader independently recalled that Mosier was taken from Sheriff Sharpless's custody and lynched (A6).

The Cheyenne Leader's two passing references (A4, A6) and the separately sourced Safety Valve narrative (A2, A3) agree that Mosier was lynched after being taken from the custody of Sheriff Sharpless, though only the retrospective narrative gives details.
